title: KPSFS Power Plant Automatic Control System
description: Kaena Point Space Force Station has a critical requirement for highly specialized engineering labor, trouble shooting, and software repair services for the failed Power Plant Automatic Control System (ACS). The scope of this effort requires the contractor to safely assess, test, evaluate, troubleshoot, and repair the localized, closed loop computer logic controller that operates the installations power plant emergency automatic control system. The repaired system must successfully achieve automated outage sensing and transition capabilities, transferring critical satellite tracking mission loads to emergency backup generators within approximately 30 seconds of a commercial grid failure. Testing must be non-destructive to ensure the total structural and software integrity of the existing generator switch gears and breakers.

title: J063, Panic and Intrusion Alarm Replacement and Monitoring, Various Clinics - Portland Veterans Affairs Healthcare System, Dept of Veterans Affairs
description: THIS IS A SOURCES SOUGHT NOTICE ONLY. This is not a solicitation for bids, proposals, proposal abstracts, or quotations. The purpose of this Sources Sought Notice is to obtain information regarding the availability and capability of all qualified sources to perform a potential requirement. The responses received from interested contractors will assist the Government in determining the appropriate acquisition method. The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), Network Contracting Office (NCO) 20, is conducting market research to identify potential sources which can provide the following services: Title: Panic and Intrusion Alarm Replacement and Monitoring NAICS Code: 561621, Security Systems Services (except Locksmiths) Locations: Fairview VA Clinic, 1800 NE Market Drive, Fairview, OR 97024 Hillsboro VA Clinic,1925 NE Stucki Ave, 3rd and 4th Floor, Hillsboro, OR, 97006 West Linn VA Clinic, 1750 SW Blankenship Road, Suite 300, West Linn, OR 97068 The Dalles CBOC, 704 Veterans Drive, The Dalles, OR 97058 Bend CBOC, 2650 NE Courtney Drive, Bend, OR, 97701 Salem CBOC, 1750 McGilchrist Street SE, Salem, OR 97302 Tasks: Within 30 days, upon award of the contract, the contractor shall remove, install, and test all new components at each location. This should include, keypads, panels, motion sensors, and wireless panic alarms, to the quantity provided at each location. Motion sensors must be based off of PIR and/or Microwave Technology. Sensors should range in detection distance of 40 to 200 feet depending on the area being covered. Some areas will require 360-degree sensors due to cross areas. Sensors should comprise of anti-masking technology where available. Once installed, Contractor shall provide alarm monitoring 24/7. All Security Systems and components must have the ability to be live tested with the monitoring station every month. This will include individual panic alarms, motion sensors, door contacts, and any other form of input. All systems must have the ability to accept multiple access codes with only one master code. The system should have the ability to track which codes were used to arm and disarm the system. The system should have the capability to be armed and disarmed with the use of a proximity card or key fob. With the possible potential to use HSPD-12 compliant ID cards, commonly known as VA PIV Badges or CAC Cards. The government should have the ability to log into the systems remotely to arm, disarm, and view activity history remotely. Contractor shall reply to repair requests within 4 hours of call. All repairs must be completed within 5 days. If not the contractor needs to supply a detailed action plan and any mitigations Period of Performance: Estimate 12/1/2025-11/30/2026 plus Option Years 1-4. Potential candidates having the capabilities necessary to provide the above stated services are invited to respond to this Sources Sought Notice via e-mail to Danielle Carrico at Danielle.Carrico@va.gov no later than 9/26/2025 at 5PM PT. No telephone inquiries will be accepted. RESPONSES SHOULD INCLUDE THE FOLLOWING INFORMATION: Company name UEI # (sam.gov) Address Business size Point of contact name, phone number, and e-mail address Capability statement GSA Federal Supply Schedule contract, if applicable Disclaimer and Important Notes: This Sources Sought Notice does not obligate the Government to award a contract or otherwise pay for the information provided in response. The Government reserves the right to use information provided by respondents for any purpose deemed necessary and legally appropriate. The Government will treat any information received as proprietary and will not share such information with other companies. Any organization responding to this Sources Sought Notice should ensure that its response is complete and sufficiently detailed to allow the Government to determine the organization's qualifications to perform the work. Respondents are advised that the Government is under no obligation to acknowledge receipt of the information received or provide feedback to respondents with respect to any information submitted. The Government may or may not issue a solicitation as a result of this announcement. There is no solicitation available at this time.

The United States Department Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), supported by the R8 Procurement and Property Support Services Division, Region 8 US Forest Service, CSA 11, intends to award on a single source basis. Purchase order type will be a Firm Fixed Price awarded to Alleghany Farm Services. This requirement is for the purchase of professional agricultural drainage construction services to install, repair, and improve subsurface drainage tile systems at the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Plant Genetic Resources Unit located at 2862 County Road 6, Geneva, New York 14456. The work includes field surveying, installation of new drainage tile, connection to existing drainage infrastructure, installation of drainage outlets and rodent guards, and use of specialized equipment to install drainage tile within vineyard and specialty crop research fields. These improvements are needed to reduce waterlogged conditions, improve soil drainage and field access, increase the amount of usable agricultural land, and support plant genetic resource conservation, regeneration, and agricultural research activities conducted at the facility. This project is essential to support the mission of the United States Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service, Plant Genetic Resources Unit by ensuring that agricultural research and germplasm regeneration fields remain accessible, productive, and suitable for crop production. The installation and improvement of subsurface drainage systems will reduce standing water and waterlogged soil conditions that currently limit planting, cultivation, maintenance, and harvesting operations. If this project is completed, poorly drained areas will continue to experience excessive soil moisture, resulting in reduced field accessibility, delayed planting and harvest operations, increased soil compaction, and degraded growing conditions. These conditions will negatively impact germplasm regeneration activities, research trials, and field-based plant breeding programs by reducing crop establishment, increasing the risk of crop loss, and compromising the quality and reliability of research data. Failure to complete the drainage improvements will also reduce the amount of usable agricultural land available for research and regeneration activities, limiting the Plant Genetic Resources Unit's capacity to maintain, regenerate, and distribute plant genetic resources. Continued deterioration of drainage conditions may result in increased maintenance costs, additional crop losses, and long-term reductions in operational efficiency. The project is therefore mission essential to maintaining critical agricultural research infrastructure and supporting the conservation and utilization of plant genetic resources entrusted to the Agricultural Research Service.

title: Consultancy: El Niño 2026 Research on Anticipatory Action for Children – Bangladesh and Somalia
description: Summary El Niño 2026 is highly likely to intensify extreme weather, hitting hardest in already fragile, crisis-aƯected contexts. Children will bear the brunt through cascading impacts on health, education, protection, and lifelong well-being, alongside significant and under-recognised loss and damage. This research will generate evidence on how these impacts unfold and how to reduce impacts and loss and damage for children, using El Niño as an entry point to inform more eƯective design, targeting, and scaling of preparedness, anticipatory action (AA) and adaptation. It will examine what works in AA, pinpointing eƯective interventions, and how systems can deliver timely, child-centred responses at scale and contribute to the evidence base for policy, financing and practice on how AA can reduce climate-related risks, losses and damages for children and strengthen resilience to future shocks. Research aim and objectives This research aims to generate actionable, child-centred evidence to inform more eƯective AA, preparedness, adaptation and responses to the 2026/26 El Niño event1 and similar climate shocks. The research is intended to inform programming and decision-making by governments, local and national actors, NGOs, donors and multilateral organisations, while contributing to wider policy and financing discussions on child-centred AA, resilience and loss and damage. It will document the loss and damage experienced by children in the context of El Niño and cumulative shocks and examine how AA can reduce the impacts on children, as well as avert, minimise and address loss and damage. The research is designed as a phased study that reflects both the anticipated progression of El Niño impacts and the time required to assess resilience and adaptation outcomes. Phase I, conducted in 2026, will focus on the immediate impacts of El Niño on children, together with an assessment of the eƯectiveness of anticipatory actions and early responses in reducing risks, losses and damages. While this phase will identify potential pathways to resilience and adaptation, it is not expected to generate suƯicient evidence to assess longer-term resilience outcomes directly. Subject to additional funding, Phase II extending the research beyond 2026, would enable analysis of longer-term and secondary impacts, as well as the contribution of anticipatory action to resilience, adaptive capacity, and vulnerability reduction for children, households and communities. The research seeks to answer the following specific questions: 1. What are the immediate and emerging impacts2 of El Niño on children? a) What impact does El Niño have on children across the most affected sectors in the selected contexts?3 b) What losses and damages do children experience as a result of El Niño and compounding shocks? c) Which children and contexts are at greatest risk? d) How do El Niño impacts interact with other climate, economic and conflict-related stressors? 2. How can anticipatory action effectively reduce the impacts experienced by children (including through actions that are timely, adequately financed, appropriately targeted, inclusive, locally led, and contextually appropriate to reduce risks, losses and damages for children)? 1 Unless otherwise stated, reference to El Niño within this document will refer to the 2026/27 event. 2 We note that impacts of the current El Niño event will extend into 2027 and in many instances may not be fully felt until considerably later. 3 Sectors could include, for example, health, education, protection and well-being; given the scope of the study, it may, however, be necessary to focus on those sectors most significantly aƯected by El Niño in the chosen geographic context, and where suƯicient relevant data is available to support meaningful analysis. 4 a) Which AA actions, modalities, and interventions are effective in mitigating negative impacts and loss and damage for children? b) What governance, coordination/capacity factors enable or constrain national and local actors in leading/sustaining effective anticipatory action? c) Which children benefit the most from interventions (e.g. age, gender, vulnerability)? d) What affects – or constrains – the effectiveness of interventions and how do these vary across contexts? e) How do different components of AA systems, including risk analysis, early warning, trigger mechanisms, pre-agreed action plans, financing, targeting and delivery, interact to shape outcomes for children? What are the key bottlenecks that constrain the timeliness, adequacy, inclusiveness, effectiveness and scale of AA? 3.
